{"id": "e14d12a6-a390-4df0-a94f-4bad4e13a700", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "chat_title", "title": "Application Load Balancer vs Network Load Balancer"}]}

{"id": "d5d7e124-53d7-48de-95c7-8b623030489f", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "The two AWS load balancer types operate at different layers and are built for different use cases:

**Application Load Balancer (ALB)**
- Operates at Layer 7 (application/HTTP layer)
- Routes traffic based on content — URL paths, hostnames, headers, query strings
- Good for microservices, container-based apps, and anything needing advanced routing (e.g., path-based or host-based routing across multiple target groups)
- Supports HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC
- Can do things like redirects, fixed responses, and authentication (via Cognito or OIDC) at the load balancer level

**Network Load Balancer (NLB)**
- Operates at Layer 4 (transport layer — TCP/UDP/TLS)
- Routes based on IP protocol data, without inspecting the actual request content
- Built for extreme performance: very low latency, can handle millions of requests per second, and supports static IP addresses / Elastic IPs per Availability Zone
- Good fit for latency-sensitive apps, non-HTTP protocols, or when clients need a fixed IP to whitelist

**In short:** reach for ALB when you need smart, content-aware routing for web applications; reach for NLB when you need raw speed, static IPs, or non-HTTP protocol support (like TCP-based services, gaming, or IoT).
